title: HANNAH PROMISED HER UNBORN SON TO GOD BEFORE SHE EVER CONCEIVED HIM
paragraphs:
HANNAH PROMISED HER UNBORN SON TO GOD BEFORE SHE EVER CONCEIVED HIM
Before Samuel had a heartbeat, Hannah had already opened her hands. And what happened next exposes one of the hardest questions of faith: Do you still want the blessing if God remains its rightful Lord?
There is something almost unbearable about Hannah’s prayer.
Not because it was eloquent.
It wasn’t.
Not because she stood before God sounding strong, composed, and spiritually impressive.
She didn’t.
She was shattered.
Her lips moved, but almost nothing came out.

And before the son she desperately wanted had lungs to breathe, fingers to wrap around hers, or a voice capable of calling her “mother,” Hannah made a promise that would eventually cost her something far deeper than the pain of waiting.
She promised the child back to God.
Read that slowly.
She surrendered Samuel before Samuel existed.
And maybe that is why her story still reaches into the places we protect from everybody else.
Because most of us know how to ask God for something.
Far fewer of us know how to place what we asked for back into His hands.
Hannah’s story begins in pain.
First Samuel tells us that Elkanah had two wives, Hannah and Peninnah. Peninnah had children. Hannah did not.
That difference became a wound.
Worse, it became ammunition.

Scripture says Hannah’s rival provoked her severely because of her barrenness. This was not a single insensitive remark that Hannah could forget by morning. The text describes recurring anguish. Year after year, when the family went to worship the LORD, the wound was reopened.
Imagine having your deepest unanswered prayer repeatedly placed beside somebody else’s answered one.
She has what you prayed for.
He received what you are still waiting for.
Their announcement appears while you are still grieving.
Their door opens while yours remains closed.
And you are trying to love God without pretending that it does not hurt.
That was Hannah.
Elkanah loved her, but even sincere human love could not repair what was happening inside her.
At one point he asked why she was weeping and why she would not eat.
But there are wounds another human being cannot love out of you.
There are rooms in the soul where even the people who genuinely love you cannot follow.
So Hannah went somewhere else.
She went before the LORD.
Scripture says she was in “bitterness of soul” and “wept sore.”
Then came the vow.
In Hebrew, 1 Samuel 1:11 begins:
וַתִּדֹּר נֶדֶר
Vattiddor neder.
Literally, the wording carries the force of “she vowed a vow.”
This was not a passing emotional thought.
Hannah was making a solemn promise before God.
Then she addressed Him:
יְהוָה צְבָאוֹת
YHWH Tseva’ot.
“The LORD of Hosts.”
The LORD of armies.
The God whose power Hannah could not manufacture, manipulate, or replace.
And then the broken woman began asking the Almighty to see her.
She pleaded that He would look upon her affliction, remember her, and not forget His servant.
Then came the sentence that changes the entire story.
If God gave her a son, she would give that son to the LORD “all the days of his life.”
Before conception...
surrender.
Before pregnancy...
consecration.
Before she heard a newborn cry...
open hands.
Hannah was asking God for something she had already determined must ultimately belong to Him.
That does not mean Christians should imitate Hannah by bargaining with God.
Her vow is a description of what Hannah did in this particular biblical moment, not a formula guaranteeing that God will grant whatever we promise to surrender.
God cannot be purchased with promises.
Prayer is not spiritual leverage.
Faith is not saying, “God, if I give You enough, You owe me what I want.”
The Gospel destroys that idea.
God owes sinners nothing, yet in Christ He gives grace we could never earn.
Hannah’s prayer is powerful for another reason.
It reveals surrender.
She wanted a son desperately, but she was willing to acknowledge that even the child she longed for would never cease to belong ultimately to God.
And there is a question hiding inside her prayer that eventually finds every believer:
What happens when the blessing arrives?
We talk often about trusting God while waiting.
But sometimes receiving is its own test.
Because it is possible to pray desperately for something and then, after receiving it, allow the gift to occupy the throne that belongs to the Giver.
We pray for the marriage...
then make the marriage our identity.
We pray for children...
then live as though they belong absolutely to us.
We pray for a business...
then let success consume the life God gave us.
We pray for influence...
then become addicted to being noticed.
We pray for provision...
then begin trusting money more than Providence.
We pray for healing...
then slowly forget the Healer.
Sometimes the most dangerous moment is not when your hands are empty.
Sometimes it is when they finally become full.
Hannah did not yet know whether those hands would ever hold a child.
She simply poured herself before God.
So intensely, in fact, that Eli the priest watched her mouth and assumed she was drunk.
Imagine that humiliation.
You finally bring your deepest pain into the presence of God...
and someone misunderstands your brokenness.
Hannah answered him:
“I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit.”
She explained that she had not been drinking.
She had been pouring out her soul before the LORD.
That sentence deserves to be remembered by anyone who has ever believed they needed polished words before approaching God.
Hannah did not perform.
She poured.
There is a difference.
Some prayers are beautifully spoken.
Others are barely spoken at all.
Some prayers sound like confidence.
Others are wet with tears.
Some prayers fill rooms.
Others are nothing more than trembling lips while the heart screams where nobody else can hear it.
God is not intimidated by the prayer you cannot make beautiful.
He does not require you to edit your grief before bringing it into His presence.

And this is where Hannah’s story becomes deeply Christ-centered—not because every detail is secretly about Jesus, but because the God to whom Hannah cried is the God whose saving purpose ultimately reaches its fullness in Christ.
Hannah needed mercy.
So do we.
Hannah could not create the answer she desired.
Neither can we create our own salvation.
And the Gospel announces something even greater than Hannah receiving Samuel.
God gave His Son.
Not because humanity negotiated successfully.
Not because sinners deserved Him.
Not because we offered God something impressive enough in exchange.
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
That is Romans 5:8.
Hannah surrendered a beloved son into the service of God.
But we must not confuse her sacrifice with the saving work of Christ.
Samuel could serve Israel.
Samuel could speak God’s word.
Samuel could become a prophet and judge.
Samuel could anoint kings.
But Samuel could not carry away the sins of the world.
Only Jesus could do that.
At Calvary, Christ did not merely demonstrate surrender.
He accomplished redemption.
The sinless Son bore sin.
The righteous One suffered for the unrighteous.
The rejected Savior opened the way for guilty people to be reconciled to God.
That is why Christianity is not ultimately the story of human beings making heroic sacrifices for God.
It is the story of God’s grace toward sinners through Jesus Christ.
And grace changes what surrender means.
We do not surrender ourselves to make God love us.
We surrender because in Christ we discover how profoundly He already has.
We do not obey to purchase forgiveness.
We obey because forgiveness was purchased by Another.
We do not give ourselves to Christ hoping our sacrifice will become sufficient.
We give ourselves to Christ because His sacrifice already is.
And Hannah’s story keeps moving.
Scripture says she eventually left, ate, and her countenance was no longer sad.
Notice the timing.
Samuel had not been conceived yet.
Nothing visible had changed.
The answer had not arrived.
But something had happened between Hannah and God.
Then Scripture gives us one of the tenderest statements in the chapter:
“The LORD remembered her.”
Biblically, this does not mean God had previously forgotten Hannah and suddenly recovered the memory.
When Scripture speaks this way of God “remembering,” it points toward God turning His covenant attention toward someone and acting according to His purpose.
In due time, Hannah conceived.
A son was born.
She named him Samuel.
The woman who once cried because her arms were empty now held the child she had begged God to give her.
Imagine the first night.
The tiny breathing.
The warmth against her chest.
The fingers.
The cries.
The sleepy eyes.
Imagine nursing the answer to the prayer that had once made you weep until you could barely speak.
And then imagine remembering your vow.
Because Hannah remembered.
That may be the part of the story we rush past too quickly.
It is easy to make promises while desperate.
Keeping them after receiving what we wanted is different.
Hannah could have rationalized.
Surely God understands.
Surely I did not mean it quite so literally.
Surely I can modify the arrangement now.
Surely this child needs me more than the sanctuary needs him.
But after Samuel was weaned, Hannah took him to Shiloh.
She returned to the place connected with her tears carrying the evidence that God had heard her.
And standing before Eli, she essentially identified herself:
I am the woman who stood here praying.
Then came the words generations of believers have remembered:
“For this child I prayed.”
But do not stop reading there.
The next movement is what makes the story so costly.
God had granted her petition, and Hannah therefore gave Samuel to the LORD.
The Hebrew of 1 Samuel 1:28 contains a beautiful wordplay built around the root שׁאל (sha’al), “to ask.”
Hannah had asked.
God had granted what was asked.
And now the child was being given over to the LORD.
The answer became an offering.
The gift did not replace the Giver.
That is where this story stops being comfortable.
Because perhaps there is something you have been clutching.
A relationship.
A child.
A dream.
A career.
A platform.
A possession.
A future you have already scripted.
Maybe you have prayed, “Lord, give this to me.”
But you have never prayed the harder prayer:
“Lord, if You give it... it is still Yours.”
And maybe the thing you need to surrender is not something beautiful.
Maybe it is the scandal.
The secret.
The compromise.
The addiction nobody knows about.
The bitterness you have fed for years.
The shame you keep dragging behind you.
The private sin you keep renaming so you do not have to repent of it.
Maybe you have become skilled at looking spiritually alive while something inside you is starving.
Hannah poured out her soul.
Perhaps it is time you stopped hiding yours.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to improve the version of you that everybody sees.
He came to save sinners.
Real sinners.
Ashamed sinners.
Compromised sinners.
Religious sinners.
Broken sinners.
People whose stories contain chapters they wish could be burned.
And that is why the Gospel is such astonishing news.
Your scandal does not have to become the final sentence.
Your failure does not have to become your identity.
Your sin must not be excused—but it can be forgiven.
Your past cannot be rewritten in the sense that it never happened—but Jesus can redeem what your past means for your future.
Repentance does not mean pretending the darkness was harmless.
It means turning from sin toward the Savior who entered our darkness to rescue us.
Grace does not call evil good.
Grace announces that Christ is mighty enough to forgive the guilty and transform the repentant.
This is why our message remains:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe you are reading this while waiting for your own “Samuel.”
Maybe you have prayed until you are tired of hearing yourself pray.
Maybe another person’s blessing has become painful to watch.
Maybe you are genuinely happy for them and quietly devastated for yourself at the same time.
Maybe you keep wondering whether God sees you.

Hannah’s story does not give us permission to promise that every barren womb will conceive, every disease will disappear, every relationship will be restored, every financial crisis will end the way we desire, or every prayer will receive the answer we imagined.
The Bible does not teach that.
What it does show us is that unanswered prayer does not make pouring out your soul to God meaningless.
God is still God in the waiting.
Christ is still sufficient when the answer is delayed.
Grace is still grace when life hurts.
And your ultimate hope cannot rest in receiving your Samuel.
It must rest in Jesus.
Because even the greatest earthly answer is temporary.
Children grow.
Careers end.
Bodies age.
Money disappears.
Applause fades.
People leave.
Earthly blessings are real, beautiful, and worthy of thanksgiving—but none of them can carry the weight of being your savior.
Jesus can.
So perhaps the deepest question in Hannah’s story is not:
“What are you asking God to give you?”
Perhaps it is:
“If God gives it, will you still worship God more than the gift?”
And there is another question.
If He does not give you exactly what you asked for...
is Jesus still enough?
That question reaches somewhere sermons sometimes cannot.
Because surrender sounds beautiful until surrender has a name.
Until it has a face.
Until it is the thing you waited years to receive.
Hannah eventually stood with Samuel at Shiloh and did what she had promised before she ever knew his face.
She opened her hands.
And what looked like an ending became part of something much larger.
Samuel would grow in the presence of the LORD.
He would hear God calling his name.
He would become one of the pivotal prophetic figures in Israel’s history.
He would minister during a crucial transition in the nation.
He would anoint Saul.
Later, he would anoint David.
And through David’s royal line, according to God’s covenant purposes, history would eventually move toward Jesus Christ, the Son of David and the true King.
Hannah could not have seen all of that when she was crying.
She only knew the pain in front of her.
That should humble us.
You do not know everything God is doing.
You do not know how far obedience may travel beyond your lifetime.
You do not know what God may do through something surrendered to Him.
But do not turn that into another prosperity formula.
Surrender does not guarantee earthly greatness.
Faithfulness does not obligate God to make your story famous.
Sometimes obedience will be known only to God.
That is enough.
Because the goal of Christianity is not becoming impressive.
It is Christ.
So bring Him the tears.
Bring Him the waiting.
Bring Him the blessing.
Bring Him the disappointment.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the child.
Bring Him the future.
Bring Him the part of yourself you keep refusing to place on the altar.
Not because surrender purchases His grace.
But because grace has finally shown you that Jesus is worth trusting with everything.
And if this exposed something you have been holding too tightly, do not hide behind a polished response.
Let somebody pray with you.
Let somebody know they are not the only Christian who has cried while trying to keep believing.
But before you leave, remember Hannah.
Remember the woman whose lips moved while nobody heard her voice.
Remember the mother who asked.
Remember the mother who received.
And remember the mother who opened her hands.
Then look toward Christ.
Because Hannah gave back the son she had prayed to receive...
but at the heart of the Gospel stands the Father who gave the Son we never could have deserved.
And Jesus willingly gave Himself for sinners.
So when your hands are empty, trust Him.
When your hands are full, worship Him.
When your heart is breaking, pour it out before Him.
When sin has stained your story, repent and run to Him.
When grace finds you, do not make an idol of the blessing.
Open your hands.
Christ is better.
And perhaps the prayer you need tonight is no longer merely, “Lord, give me what I desperately want.”
Perhaps it is:
“Lord Jesus, whether You give, withhold, restore, redirect, or ask me to release what I love, keep my heart Yours.”
Because sometimes the greatest evidence that grace has changed us is not that God finally placed something in our hands...
but that Jesus became precious enough for us to open them.
